name: Osteonecrosis of the Jaw

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons (AAOMS) Diagnostic Criteria

criteria.description: Exposed bone or bone that can be probed through an intraoral or extraoral fistula in the maxillofacial region persisting for more than 8 weeks
No history of radiation therapy to the jaws
Current or previous treatment with antiresorptive or antiangiogenic agents
Localized pain or swelling in the jaw region
Radiographic evidence of osteolysis or sclerosis in the affected jaw

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of exposed bone or bone probeable through fistula persisting >8 weeks, no history of radiation therapy to jaws, and current or previous antiresorptive/antiangiogenic therapy
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes of jaw necrosis such as osteomyelitis or malignancy.

pathognomonic.notes: Exposed bone visible intraorally or extraorally
searchTerms: jaw bone exposed and not healing

pathognomonic.notes: Fistula tract allowing probing to bone

common.symptomName: Swelling of the affected jaw region
common.notes: Soft tissue swelling adjacent to necrotic bone

common.symptomName: Loosening of teeth adjacent to necrotic bone
searchTerms: teeth loosening around jaw bone damage

common.notes: Due to necrotic tissue and secondary infection

occasional.symptomName: Pus discharge from intraoral or extraoral fistula
searchTerms: pus coming from mouth or skin fistula
discharge from oral or facial fistula

occasional.symptomName: Numbness or paresthesia of the lower lip or chin (mental nerve neuropathy)
occasional.notes: Due to nerve involvement or compression
searchTerms: numbness in lower lip or chin
tingling or loss of feeling in chin area

laboratory: Elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) in secondary infection
Normal or mildly elevated white blood cell count
imaging: Radiolucent areas indicating osteolysis on panoramic radiograph
Sclerosis and thickening of cortical bone on CT scan
Sequestra and periosteal reaction visible on imaging
other: History of bisphosphonate, denosumab, or antiangiogenic therapy
Clinical examination revealing exposed necrotic bone

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of systemic infection signs more prominent
No history of antiresorptive or antiangiogenic therapy
Bone exposure may be transient and responds to antibiotics
History of radiation therapy to the head and neck region
Presence of ulcerative or exophytic mass

redFlags: Progressive bone necrosis despite conservative management
Signs of deep space infection or cellulitis
references: Ruggiero SL, Dodson TB, Fantasia J, et al. American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons position paper on medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw—2014 update. J Oral Maxillofac Surg. 2014;72(10):1938-1956.

Khosla S, Burr D, Cauley J, et al. Bisphosphonate-associated osteonecrosis of the jaw: report of a task force of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. J Bone Miner Res. 2007;22(10):1479-1491.
Ruggiero SL. Osteonecrosis of the jaw and bisphosphonate therapy. J Oral Maxillofac Surg. 2004;62(11):1308-1311.
